subtitle: How a sender keeps the wire busy without drowning the receiver, recovers from loss, and shares a cable with others.

sw.body:
The most polite way for you to talk is to say a sentence and then wait for “mm-hm” before the next one. That is stop-and-wait, the simplest kind of ARQ (automatic repeat request). The receiver acknowledges good frames and the sender retransmits after a timeout. It sends one frame, waits for its ACK, then sends the next. It is correct and trivial, but the link sits idle for a whole round trip per frame.

How bad is it? On a 1 Mb/s link with 1000-bit frames and a one-way delay of 20 ms, the frame time is 1 ms and the round trip 40 ms. Utilisation = frame time / (frame time + RTT) = 1/(1 + 40) ≈ 2.4%. In the figure four frames take 16 time units, each waiting for its own acknowledgement. So why is stop-and-wait poor on a long fast link? The sender spends nearly all its time waiting.
keynotes: ARQ: the receiver acknowledges good frames and the sender retransmits after a timeout.
Stop-and-wait sends one frame and waits for its ACK, leaving the link idle for a whole round trip per frame.
On a 1 Mb/s link with 1000-bit frames and 20 ms one-way delay, utilisation is 1/(1 + 40) ≈ 2.4%.

window.body:
Waiting after every frame wastes the wire, as you saw. A better idea: keep sending, and let the acknowledgements catch up. A sliding window lets the sender have up to W unacknowledged frames in flight. But what happens when one of them is lost? There are two answers.

Go-Back-N: the receiver accepts only the next expected frame, so one loss forces the sender to resend that frame and all after it. Selective Repeat: the receiver buffers out-of-order frames and acknowledges each, so only the lost frame is resent. With window 4 and frame 2 lost, Go-Back-N retransmits 4 frames, Selective Repeat just 1. See both in the figures. Go-Back-N resends frames that arrived safely because the receiver threw them away for being out of order.
keynotes: A sliding window lets the sender have up to W unacknowledged frames in flight.
Go-Back-N: the receiver accepts only the next expected frame, so a loss forces a resend of that frame and all after it; Selective Repeat buffers out-of-order frames, so only the lost frame is resent.
With window 4 and frame 2 lost, Go-Back-N retransmits 4 frames and Selective Repeat just 1.

mac.body:
Put many people in one room with one microphone, and you get chaos unless there are rules. That is the problem of a shared cable: when many stations share a medium, collisions happen. The oldest answer is Pure ALOHA: transmit whenever you like, giving a maximum throughput of 18.4% (1/2e). Slotted ALOHA transmits only at slot starts, doubling it to 36.8% (1/e).

Better manners: CSMA listens first. CSMA/CD (Ethernet) also listens while sending and aborts on a collision, then waits a random back-off that doubles each time. CSMA/CA (Wi-Fi) cannot hear collisions, so it avoids them with random waits and acknowledgements. The maths: pure ALOHA throughput S = G·e^(−2G) peaks at G = 0.5, giving S = 0.5e⁻¹ ≈ 0.184. Slotted ALOHA S = G·e^(−G) peaks at G = 1, giving e⁻¹ ≈ 0.368. Why can Wi-Fi not use collision detection? A radio cannot listen while it transmits.
keynotes: Pure ALOHA transmits whenever it likes and peaks at 18.4% (1/2e); slotted ALOHA transmits only at slot starts and peaks at 36.8% (1/e).
CSMA listens first; CSMA/CD (Ethernet) aborts on a collision and waits a random back-off that doubles each time; CSMA/CA (Wi-Fi) avoids collisions with random waits and acknowledgements.
Pure ALOHA S = G·e^(−2G) peaks at G = 0.5; slotted ALOHA S = G·e^(−G) peaks at G = 1.

switching.body:
Modern Ethernet got rid of the shared cable altogether. A switch gives every port its own collision domain, so modern Ethernet is full duplex and needs no CSMA/CD. And you can go one step further with a VLAN, which splits one physical switch into several logical LANs. Frames carry an 802.1Q tag with a VLAN id, and only a router moves traffic between VLANs.

Why do this? To isolate departments, limit broadcasts and apply security. In the figure, A and B talk directly, but A and C must go through the router. Hosts in different VLANs on the same switch can talk only via a router.
keynotes: A switch gives every port its own collision domain, so modern Ethernet is full duplex and needs no CSMA/CD.
A VLAN splits one physical switch into several logical LANs; frames carry an 802.1Q tag with a VLAN id.
Only a router moves traffic between VLANs; uses include isolating departments, limiting broadcasts and applying security.

eff.body:
How full is your pipe? A simple formula tells you. Link utilisation with a window of W frames is U = W × tframe / (tframe + RTT), capped at 1. The bandwidth × delay product tells you how many bits are needed in flight to fill the pipe, so choose W at least that many frames.

Work through it. A 100 Mb/s link, 1250-byte frames (10 000 bits), RTT 10 ms. The frame time = 10 000 / 10⁸ = 0.1 ms, and RTT / frame time = 100. The window needed to fill the pipe is 1 + 100 = 101 frames. With W = 7, utilisation is only 7 / 101 ≈ 6.9%. Bandwidth × delay tells you how much data must be in flight to keep the link busy.
keynotes: Utilisation with a window of W frames is U = W × t_frame / (t_frame + RTT), capped at 1.
Bandwidth × delay tells you how many bits must be in flight to fill the pipe.
For 100 Mb/s, 10 000-bit frames and RTT 10 ms, 101 frames fill the pipe; W = 7 gives only 7/101 ≈ 6.9%.

summary.body:
Three lines to take away.

  • Sliding windows keep the pipe full; window ≥ 1 + RTT/frame-time.
  • GBN resends the window; SR resends only the lost frame.
  • CSMA/CD detects, CSMA/CA avoids.
keynotes: Sliding windows keep the pipe full; the window should be at least 1 + RTT/frame-time.
Go-Back-N resends the window and Selective Repeat resends only the lost frame.
CSMA/CD detects collisions and CSMA/CA avoids them.
